prompt: Why didn't Harvard have calculus classes when it first opened?
answer:
Harvard did not offer calculus when it opened because **calculus had not yet been developed**. Harvard was founded in 1636 and began operating in 1638, while Newton and Leibniz developed the foundations of differential and integral calculus only in the 1660s–1680s.

There was also a broader curricular reason. Early Harvard modeled itself on English universities, whose curriculum emphasized classical subjects such as Latin, Greek, rhetoric, logic, theology, and philosophy. Mathematics was regarded largely as practical knowledge for mechanics and navigation, not as a central subject for educated students. During Harvard’s seventeenth century, students generally studied only arithmetic and plane and spherical geometry—and even those mainly in their senior year. Algebra did not appear in the curriculum until about 1721.

Once calculus became available and suitable textbooks circulated, Harvard gradually introduced it. By the early nineteenth century students could study “fluxions” (an early name for calculus), and calculus became more prominent under professors such as John Farrar and Benjamin Peirce.
